findings.suppression_reason: JamesWoolfenden/.github is the same author's own repo; @main accepted as a self-controlled trust root rather than pinned to a SHA. Suppressed alongside HLD_CI_017 via inline # holden:ignore comments in verify.yml and pull_request.yml.
findings.title: CI identity reachable via mutable-ref reusable workflow holds setIamPolicy on the CMEK key and the repository
findings.explanation: Both workflows call JamesWoolfenden/.github/.github/workflows/terraform-{verify,pr}-gcp.yml@main (HLD_CI_017 already flags the mutable ref) impersonating terraform-gcp-artifact-reposit@pike-477416.iam.gserviceaccount.com. That identity's own least-privilege role, defined in .pike/pike.generated_policy.tf lines 8-16, includes cloudkms.cryptoKeys.setIamPolicy and artifactregistry.repositories.setIamPolicy. Both are full-policy-replace permissions (GCP has no narrower 'add one binding' permission), so whoever controls the JamesWoolfenden/.github main branch can, through this pipeline, replace the entire IAM policy on the CMEK key protecting every artifact in the registry and on the registry itself — e.g. grant an arbitrary principal cloudkms.admin or artifactregistry.admin — not merely run Terraform plans/applies against the resources this module defines. This deepens HLD_CI_017's generic 'authenticate to cloud provider' rationale with the specific blast radius for this repo: compromise of one mutable ref in an unrelated repo escalates to full control of confidentiality (KMS) and access control (registry) for this module's managed resources.
findings.remediation: Pin both job-level uses: to the resolved commit SHA of terraform-verify-gcp.yml/terraform-pr-gcp.yml (fixes HLD_CI_017 and closes this path). Separately, verify branch protection is enforced on JamesWoolfenden/.github's main branch, since it is a trust root for every repo that calls into it. setIamPolicy itself can't be narrowed further while these Terraform IAM member resources exist — that's an inherent GCP API constraint, not a fixable over-grant — so the practical mitigation is closing the ref-pinning gap, not editing the custom role.

findings.suppression_reason: False positive: local.service_robot is the Cloud Run/App Engine serverless robot, and Google's documented pattern for serverless products pulling images from a CMEK-protected Artifact Registry repo requires granting that same identity both roles/artifactregistry.reader (pull the image) and the KMS decrypt role (decrypt it) — one purpose, not two unrelated grants. Confirmed by the user.
findings.title: CMEK service agent is folded into the repository's reader membership, not just granted key-decrypt access
findings.explanation: `local.members = concat(var.members, [local.service_robot])` folds the Artifact Registry CMEK service agent (serviceAccount:service-${var.project_id}@serverless-robot-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com) into the same list that drives google_artifact_registry_repository_iam_member.users' for_each, so that Google-managed service identity ends up holding roles/artifactregistry.reader on the repository in addition to the roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter grant it already gets from google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.pike. Those two grants serve different purposes (decrypt-at-rest for the backend vs. registry-content read for a consumer), and holden's HLD_GCP_210 doesn't catch this because the member resolves to a recognised service-agent pattern rather than a flagged literal, so it reads as an intentional grant, not a gap. I can't rule out that GCP's Artifact Registry CMEK flow genuinely requires reader access on the repo in addition to decrypt on the key — that's account/provider behaviour outside the IaC — so this is flagged at low confidence as worth double-checking rather than a confirmed over-grant.
findings.remediation: Confirm whether the Artifact Registry service agent needs roles/artifactregistry.reader on the repository for CMEK reads to work, or whether the existing roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter grant on the key is sufficient by itself. If reader access isn't required, keep local.service_robot out of local.members and grant it only via google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.pike.

findings.title: Repository creation can race KMS IAM propagation on first apply
findings.explanation: The repository's kms_key_name references a CMEK key, and `depends_on = [google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.pike]` orders the IAM grant's apply before the repository's. depends_on only orders the Terraform apply graph, though — it doesn't wait for the grant to actually propagate through GCP's IAM backend, which is documented as eventually consistent (commonly 30-60s). If repository creation is attempted before the grant has propagated, GCP validates CMEK access against the service agent at create time and the apply can fail with a transient permission-denied error that clears on a plain re-apply, with no retry/wait logic in this module to absorb it.
findings.remediation: Add a short wait between the IAM grant and the repository create — e.g. a time_sleep resource keyed off google_kms_crypto_key_iam_member.pike and referenced from the repository's depends_on — or document that a transient first-apply failure is expected and a re-apply resolves it.

findings.title: README issue-tracker links point at an unrelated repo (terraform-aws-bigquery), leftover from a template
findings.explanation: Lines 116 and 122 both link to https://github.com/jameswoolfenden/terraform-aws-bigquery/issues instead of this repo's own tracker. The rest of the README (badges, inputs/outputs tables, role tables) is specific to terraform-gcp-artifact-repository, so these two links read as unedited leftovers from whatever template this README was copied from — the same stale-template-link pattern just found and fixed in the sibling terraform-gcp-artifact-reader repo's README, which pointed at a different wrong repo (terraform-aws-cluster). holden has no check over README prose, so this is invisible to the deterministic engine.
